https://www.dw.com/en/philippines-studen.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iz4R Two students, including the shooter, have been killed and at least two others wounded at a campus in Zamboanga. Image: AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A high school student opened fire at a private university campus in the Philippines on Tuesday, killing a fellow student and wounding two others before turning the gun on himself. The shooting, which the student reportedly livestreamed using a body camera, took place at about 7:50 a.m. local time at Ateneo de Zamboanga University in the southern port city of Zamboanga, about 800 kilometers (500 miles) south of the capital, Manila . Hundreds of students were evacuated after gunshots were heard in the high school building, which is located on a secure campus separate from the university's main campus. Regional police said a ninth-grade student, typically ages 14-16, brought a "pistol and rifle inside the school campus" and opened fire in a classroom. "One of the focuses our investigation will look into is how the suspect brought the firearms into the school," said a spokeswoman. "The investigation is ongoing ... We are still trying to identify the motive." A few hours after the shooting, police said the situation was under control. They requested that parents and guardians of students remain calm and follow advice issued by the school to pick up their children. Police chief Jose Melencio Nartatez also called on the public to "refrain from sharing unconfirmed reports, photos, or videos that may cause unnecessary concern," adding that authorities would "provide verified information as appropriate." People gathered outside the Ateneo de Zamboanga University campus following the shooting. Classes at the university were suspended. Image: Nonoy Lacson/REUTERS Philippines: How did the shooting unfold? In a video that was seemingly livestreamed on Facebook and circulated by local media, the barrel of a gun is seen moving down a hallway in the style of a first-person shooter video game before being aimed into a classroom and fired, according to the AFP news agency. "In the video, we see that he first shot at the teacher who was sitting at a desk," Zamboanga city mayor Khymer Olaso told a local radio station. "It seems he missed, then moved to another room [and] shot another student there." Other children in school uniforms can reportedly be seen screaming and rushing for an exit. The alleged shooter's Facebook account has since been disabled, and classes at the university were suspended. Are school shootings common in the Philippines? School shootings are rare in the Philippines where gun ownership is tightly regulated. However, a large black market for firearms exists, and three students were killed while 20 others were injured in a shooting in the eastern city of Tacloban in June. Last month, the Ateneo de Zamboanga campus became one of many educational institutions across the country to conduct active-shooter drills. "We are all aware that security measures have been stepped up in schools," said the police spokeswoman. Edited by: Louis Oelofse Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Potholes along a road in regional Victoria. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding a crash on the Western Highway at Trawalla that left a Ballarat man dead. Photograph: James Ross/AAP View image in fullscreen Potholes along a road in regional Victoria. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding a crash on the Western Highway at Trawalla that left a Ballarat man dead. Photograph: James Ross/AAP Victoria Motorcyclist’s death reignites debate over potholes on Victoria’s ‘deteriorating’ roads Coalition says potholes must be fixed ‘as a matter of urgency’ after 71-year-old crashed and died on Western Highway at Trawalla, west of Ballarat, on Sunday Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press and Benita Kolovos Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.44 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 20.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Emergency services were called to Trawalla, west of Ballarat, shortly before 1pm on Sunday after reports a motorcycle had struck a pothole. The 71-year-old rider, from Ballarat, died at the scene after reportedly losing control on the Western Highway, near Trawalla Road. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the crash, which are yet to be determined. But the incident has revived concerns about the quality of Victoria’s public roads, an issue which is shaping up to be a key election flashpoint . Labor has had 12 years to fix Victorian roads. Turning to ‘pothole populism’ now may be too late Read more A report from the Victorian auditor general on 9 September found 48% of the network was in poor or very poor condition. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email This was up from 39% in 2021. Examining more than 23,000 kilometres of state roads, it characterised the overall condition of Victoria’s public roads as “deteriorating”. The Victorian Coalition has pledged $5bn over four years to plug 1m potholes and re-establish preventive road maintenance. The Labor government, meanwhile, has committed $352m to double the number of potholes fixed in 2026 from 250,000 to 500,000. In a statement the premier, Ben Carroll, described the incident as “a tragic loss of life” and said “road conditions aren’t good enough”. “Victoria police have been clear that the circumstances are still under investigation, so I’m not going to pre-empt that,” he said. Speaking on ABC radio, Carroll said “the buck does stop with us”. “I’ve made it very clear there cannot be any more buck passing on road maintenance. That’s why I have said, under my government – it was outsourced in the mid-1990s – I’m going to bring road maintenance back inside of government.” The shadow minister for roads and road safety, Danny O’Brien, said the death was “the saddest possible consequence to have come from the terrible state of Victorian roads and it should never have come to this”. “These potholes need to be fixed and fixed properly as a matter of urgency. It is time for action and this needs to be the highest priority now so that no more lives are lost on Victorian roads because of government neglect,” he said. O’Brien said the Liberals and Nationals would continue to press the government to bring forward road maintenance works for regional Victoria’s most dangerous roads. The Victorian state election is due to be held on 28 November. On 3 September 2026, during a working visit to Italy, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, delivered a lecture at the NATO Defence College and gave interviews to the Italian news agency Agenzia Nova and the Italian television channels SKY and TG2POST . The Minister also met with the President of the Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee of the Italian Senate, Maurizio Gasparri. On 4 September, the Minister accompanied Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs on his visit to the Holy See. During the meeting at the Senate, the officials discussed cooperation between Latvia and Italy in the areas of security and defence. The Minister expressed her gratitude for Italy's military presence in Latvia and its participation in NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission. Baiba Braže particularly highlighted the effective work of Italy's Eurofighter jets, which shot down an unmanned aerial vehicle that had entered Latvian airspace from Belarus on 14 August. The Minister also provided an update on the security situation in the region, Russia's hybrid aggression and Belarus's instrumentalisation of migration. She expressed appreciation for Italy's support for Ukraine and called for maintaining a focus on comprehensive assistance to Ukraine. The Minister stressed the need to maintain the international isolation of Russia, which poses a long-term threat to Europe, and to ensure that Russia is held accountable for its war of aggression in Ukraine. During discussions on strengthening Europe's defence capabilities and the EU Multiannual Financial Framework, the Minister emphasised the need to ensure sufficient funding to strengthen the EU's eastern border - a shared responsibility of NATO and the EU. The parties agreed that stability in the east and south is equally important. The Minister expressed solidarity with Italy regarding the challenges posed by migration. The parties exchanged views on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and international efforts to restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. In a lecture at the NATO Defence College, the Minister shared Latvia's perspective on the future of the Alliance, the threats posed by Russia, and Latvia's contribution to strengthening national defence since Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The Minister also met with the College's leadership - Commandant Lieutenant General Jérôme Goisque and the Dean, Deputy Commandant Suzanne Nielsen. Baiba Braže is the first foreign minister to be received at the College by Commandant Goisque since he took office in July this year. During the visit, the Minister gave three interviews - to the news agency Agenzia Nova and the Italian television channels SKY and TG2POST - outlining current developments in bilateral cooperation between Latvia and Italy, the security situation in the Baltic region, with a special emphasis on the challenges along the eastern border, and sharing Latvia's perspective on EU enlargement policy and the strengthening of European defence capabilities. On 4 September, she participated in Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs' visit to the Holy See, where an audience with His Holiness Pope Leo XIV and a meeting with the Secretary of State of the Holy See, His Eminence Cardinal Pietro Parolin, took place. During the meeting with Cardinal Parolin, the Minister discussed the role of Vatican diplomacy in achieving a just and lasting peace in Ukraine.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A Ukrainian couple and their baby daughter outside a bombed building in Kyiv on Tuesday. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP View image in fullscreen A Ukrainian couple and their baby daughter outside a bombed building in Kyiv on Tuesday. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Ukraine Analysis In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Throttling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holds Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.54 EDT Last modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.55 EDT Share In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns. Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued. Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph). Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate. View image in fullscreen The aftermath of a Russian missile attack in Kyiv on Wednesday. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia . However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental. Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.” However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink , a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military. So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine. The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office. “You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored. A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening. Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv , gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front. Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders. “There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques. Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force. The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger. As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.” Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.
